findings.claim: Clemenceau “had been just 29 when Germany invaded France in 1871”.
findings.truth: Clemenceau was born on 28 September 1841. The Franco-Prussian invasion of France began in July 1870, when he was 28; the German Empire did not yet exist in 1870.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Georges Clemenceau' (born 28 September 1841; returned to Paris after Sedan, 1870)

findings.claim: Timeline: “32 nations meet at Versailles” in January 1919.
findings.truth: The Paris Peace Conference met in Paris; Versailles was where the treaty with Germany was signed in June 1919. The lesson's own key fact says the conference was in Paris.
findings.evidence: spec BB part one 'The armistice: aims of the peacemakers'; Wikipedia 'Treaty of Versailles'

findings.claim: “the USA … suffered around 100,000 casualties” and “Over 1.4 million French soldiers were killed”.
findings.truth: US military deaths were about 116,500 and total US casualties about 320,000; French military dead are usually given as about 1.4 million, so 'over 1.4 million' is at the top of the range. Both are within normal textbook tolerance.

findings.claim: The <dfn> and the glossary define “Rhineland” as “A zone where no military forces or fortifications are permitted.”
findings.truth: That is the definition of a demilitarised zone. The Rhineland is the German region on the western border facing France and Belgium - which is how lesson 11 defines it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Remilitarization of the Rhineland'; lesson 11 of this unit

findings.claim: The Rhineland “was demilitarised and occupied by French troops.”
findings.truth: The Rhineland was occupied by Allied forces - British, French, Belgian and (to 1923) American - for fifteen years under the treaty.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Treaty of Versailles' (Rhineland occupation, 15 years, Allied forces)

findings.claim: “West Prussia, Upper Silesia, and Posen were given to Poland.”
findings.truth: The treaty ordered a plebiscite in Upper Silesia. It was held on 20 March 1921 (59.6% for Germany) and the region was partitioned in October 1921. Lesson 6 of this unit teaches that partition as a League success, so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Upper Silesia plebiscite'; lesson 6 of this unit

findings.claim: The Polish Corridor gave “Poland access to the sea at Danzig (a German city)”.
findings.truth: Danzig was made a Free City under League of Nations protection on 15 November 1920; it was neither Polish nor part of the Corridor. This lesson's own mark scheme says Danzig was placed 'under League control', and lesson 14 calls it a Free City.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Free City of Danzig'; lesson 14 of this unit

findings.claim: Mark schemes in lessons 2, 3 and 4 state the reparations split as “France would receive 50% (they had wanted 70%), Britain 30%”.
findings.truth: The Spa Conference of July 1920 is normally given as France 52%, the British Empire 22%, Italy 10%, Belgium 8% and 8% to the rest. Two defensible options: (a) correct the figures to 52/22 across four mark schemes, or (b) drop the percentages and keep only the £6.6 billion total. I could not confirm the Spa figures from a fetchable source in this session, so I have not written the edit.
findings.evidence: no fetchable source confirmed (Wikipedia 'World War I reparations' and 'Reparations Commission' do not give the Spa shares)

findings.claim: “Germany lost 26% of its coal and half of its iron and steel resources.”
findings.truth: Sources vary widely on the coal figure: Wikipedia's Weimar Republic article gives 10% of coal and 48% of iron; other standard summaries give 16% or 26%. The iron/steel half matches 48%. Left alone: the figure recurs eight times and in a knowledge-check answer key, and I could not establish a single true value.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Weimar Republic' (48% of iron, 10% of coal resources)

findings.claim: The glossary repeats 'reparations' and 'War Guilt Clause' (lesson 2) and 'collective security' (lesson 5).
findings.truth: Duplicate glossary rows - a data defect, not a factual error.

findings.claim: “Clemenceau lost the general election shortly after the Treaty was signed.”
findings.truth: Clemenceau did not lose a general election. His Bloc National won the legislative elections of November 1919. He stood for the presidency, lost the preliminary caucus to Paul Deschanel on 16 January 1920, withdrew, and resigned as Prime Minister on 17 January 1920.

findings.claim: Keynes “wrote The Economic Consequences of Peace (1919)” - repeated in the knowledge-check stem.
findings.truth: The book is The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'The Economic Consequences of the Peace'

findings.claim: Keynes is quoted as “calling the Big Three ‘greedy and weak’” - repeated as the knowledge-check stem.
findings.truth: Keynes used no such phrase. His portraits attack Wilson as slow and ill-informed, Clemenceau as vindictive and Lloyd George as a manipulator. An invented quotation attributed to a named author.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'The Economic Consequences of the Peace' (Keynes's characterisations)

findings.claim: “The US Congress refused to ratify the Treaty”.
findings.truth: The Senate ratifies treaties, and it was the Senate that rejected Versailles. Lesson 1 of this unit says 'the US Senate' correctly.
findings.evidence: US Constitution Article II; lesson 1 of this unit

findings.claim: “France invaded the Ruhr” in 1923.
findings.truth: French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr from January 1923. A common shorthand, not worth an edit.

findings.claim: “Mustafa Kemal Atatürk” leading the revolt of 1919-23.
findings.truth: He took the surname Atatürk only in 1934; at the time he was Mustafa Kemal. Harmless for a GCSE answer.

findings.claim: “Wilson lost the 1920 election to Warren Harding” - and twice more inside mark schemes.
findings.truth: Wilson was not a candidate in 1920. He had suffered a stroke in October 1919; Harding defeated the Democratic candidate James M. Cox.

findings.claim: “The USSR was banned because it was communist … Germany was banned until it proved it was peaceful.”
findings.truth: Neither was banned. Both were excluded at the start and both later joined: Germany on 8 September 1926 (taught in lesson 7) and the USSR on 18 September 1934. The USSR was expelled only in December 1939.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Member states of the League of Nations'

findings.claim: “support the Court of International Justice”.
findings.truth: Its name was the Permanent Court of International Justice, as the same lesson says two paragraphs later.

findings.claim: The four permanent Council members “each with veto power”.
findings.truth: Council decisions needed the agreement of every member present, so temporary members also held an effective veto. A standard GCSE simplification.

findings.claim: The description promises “Dawes/Young Plans”.
findings.truth: The Young Plan is never mentioned anywhere in the lesson. The description should name only what the lesson teaches.

findings.claim: “The Dawes Plan (1924) had stabilised Germany’s economy by providing US loans, ending the hyperinflation crisis” - repeated in a mark scheme.
findings.truth: Hyperinflation was ended by the currency reform of November 1923 (the Rentenmark), nine months before the Dawes Plan of August 1924. The Dawes Plan stabilised the economy after it.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Dawes Plan'; 'Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic'

findings.claim: The Kellogg-Briand Pact “was signed in August 1928 … Signed by 62 nations”.
findings.truth: Fifteen states signed on 27 August 1928; the rest adhered later, reaching roughly 57-62 by 1929. The lesson merges the two. The figure 62 also sits in a knowledge-check answer key, so changing it ripples.

findings.claim: The Locarno Treaties “were signed in October 1925 in Switzerland”.
findings.truth: They were negotiated and initialled at Locarno in October 1925 but formally signed in London on 1 December 1925. Standard textbook shorthand.

findings.claim: Japan “walked out of the League (March 1933) and then invaded Jehol”.
findings.truth: The Jehol operation began on 23 February 1933, the day before the Assembly vote; Japan's delegation walked out on 24 February and gave formal notice on 27 March. The order is reversed by days, not years.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Operation Nekka'; 'Member states of the League of Nations'

findings.claim: Japan placed Pu Yi “on the throne” of Manchukuo in 1932.
findings.truth: He was installed as Chief Executive in March 1932 and became emperor only in 1934.

findings.claim: “In June 1935, he spoke at the League in Geneva, warning of what would happen if they failed to act” - with a matching timeline entry and revision tip.
findings.truth: Haile Selassie did not appear at Geneva in 1935. He addressed the Assembly in 1936, after Italy had conquered his country - the very speech this lesson describes correctly a few paragraphs later. In 1935 Abyssinia appealed and the League talked while Italy built up its forces.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Haile Selassie' (allowed to address the assembly in 1936, after the invasion)

findings.claim: “Italy conquered Abyssinia in May 1936 and then left the League” - in the prose, the timeline, a knowledge-check stem and two model answers.
findings.truth: Italy withdrew from the League on 11 December 1937. The mark schemes in lessons 6 and 9 of this same unit say 'Italy (1937)', so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Member states of the League of Nations' (Italy: joined 10 January 1920, withdrew 11 December 1937)

findings.claim: Abyssinia “was the only independent black country in Africa”.
findings.truth: Liberia was independent as well. Abyssinia was one of only two.

findings.claim: The Anglo-German Naval Agreement allowed “a navy up to 35% of the Royal Navy — including submarines”.
findings.truth: The 35% cap applied to surface tonnage; submarines were allowed at 45% of British submarine tonnage, rising to parity on notice. The headline 35% is right.

findings.claim: The Saar had been “run by the League since 1919”.
findings.truth: League administration began when the treaty came into force on 10 January 1920 and ran fifteen years to the 1935 plebiscite.

findings.claim: “In 1940, Guilty Men blamed Chamberlain but mainly blamed Hitler. In 1961, A.J.P. Taylor argued that Chamberlain’s misreading of the situation pushed Hitler into war.”
findings.truth: Guilty Men (1940) blamed Chamberlain and the appeasers - it is the founding text of that case and did not shift blame to Hitler. Taylor's 1961 thesis was that Hitler was an opportunist and the war came from blunders on all sides; he was largely sympathetic to Chamberlain. Lesson 10 of this unit states Taylor's position correctly, so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Guilty Men'; 'The Origins of the Second World War'; lesson 10 of this unit

findings.claim: At Munich “Hitler got all his demands”.
findings.truth: Munich gave him the Sudetenland but on a staged handover from 1 to 10 October, not the immediate occupation he had demanded at Bad Godesberg.

findings.claim: The secret protocol “gave Stalin a sphere of influence over the Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) and parts of Finland”.
findings.truth: The protocol of 23 August 1939 put Finland (all of it), Estonia, Latvia and Bessarabia in the Soviet sphere and Lithuania in the German sphere. Lithuania moved to the Soviet sphere only under the second protocol of 28 September 1939.

findings.claim: “In return, Stalin sent Germany 30 warplanes and samples of other weapons.”
findings.truth: The direction is reversed. Under the German-Soviet commercial agreements Germany supplied the USSR with samples of thirty of its latest warplanes (Bf 109, Bf 110, Ju 88, Do 215) plus naval and industrial equipment, in exchange for Soviet oil, grain and raw materials.

findings.claim: Of the Polish army, “Much of it relied on horse-mounted cavalry and outdated equipment”.
findings.truth: Poland fielded eleven cavalry brigades within a mainly infantry army. Its equipment was outdated, but cavalry was a small part of it - the 'Poland fought tanks with horses' image is a propaganda myth.

findings.claim: A revision tip asks students to “name the operation used to stage the Gleiwitz Incident”.
findings.truth: The answer (Operation Himmler) is never given anywhere in the lesson, so the tip cannot be answered from the text.

findings.claim: Of the Hossbach Memorandum: “He named Austria, Czechoslovakia, Poland, and Lithuania as targets, and said this must happen as soon as possible.”
findings.truth: The record names Austria and Czechoslovakia as the targets and sets a timetable of five or six years (1943-45 at the latest). Poland and Lithuania come from Hugh Trevor-Roper's later reading of the document, not from the minute.

findings.claim: In every one of the 15 lessons, flashcards 4 and 5 are auto-generated cloze fragments cut from headings and body text: answers with the punctuation stripped out (“Hitlers”, “NaziSoviet”, “Leagues”), answers that are not facts at all (“Case”, “From”, “Steps”, “Mixed”, “Growing”), answers printed inside their own question (“David”, “League”, “Hitler”, “Gleiwitz”), and questions that are not questions.
findings.truth: 30 cards. All replaced with a real question and a real answer drawn from the same lesson, unique within each deck.
findings.evidence: the raw rows themselves; flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: In every one of the 15 lessons, flashcards 1-3 are bare glossary definitions on the front with the term on the back, so the prompt is never phrased as a question.
findings.truth: 45 cards. Each front rewritten as a 'Which term/word/treaty …?' question with the same answer.
findings.evidence: flashcard rules in the checker brief

findings.claim: All 15 lesson descriptions run over the 100-character validator limit (103 to 118 characters).
findings.truth: Only lesson 7's description is rewritten here (94 characters), because it was also inaccurate. The other 14 need a separate trim pass - none of them is factually wrong.

summary: Checked against the spec: this option is BB, Conflict and tension: the inter-war years, 1918-1939, and Paper 1 is a two-hour, 84-mark exam worth 50% with four compulsory questions in this section - source analysis 4, how useful are two sources 12, write an account 8, and a 16-mark judgement essay carrying the 4 spelling, punctuation and grammar marks. Every practice question in the unit uses one of those forms with the right marks, the band labels avoid the banned wording, and no lesson names the board. The factual errors cluster in the reactions, the League and the Abyssinian lessons: Clemenceau losing a general election he never fought, Wilson losing a 1920 election he never stood in, Keynes's book retitled and given an invented quotation, Haile Selassie speaking at Geneva a year early, Italy leaving the League in 1936 instead of December 1937, and the Nazi-Soviet aircraft traffic running the wrong way. Four of those contradict statements the unit itself makes elsewhere, and three had spread into knowledge-check stems or model answers. Separately, the flashcard decks are broken unit-wide: 30 of the 75 cards are auto-generated cloze fragments and the other 45 are bare definitions with no question. One item is left for adjudication: the reparations split given as France 50% and Britain 30%, which is usually 52% and 22%, but I could not confirm the Spa Conference figures from a fetchable source. Lessons 4, 6, 8, 10 and 11 need no factual fix - only low notes - though their flashcards are rebuilt like the rest.
